svg.title: Radar, transponder and ADS-B: what ATC sees
svg.desc: Primary radar times radio pulses but has limits: signals degrade over distance, cannot pass through mountains, and the fastest radar updates every 4.7 seconds. ATCRBS adds an interrogator, transponder and radarscope. A transponder code is four numbers from 0 to 7, giving 4,096 possible codes, and ATC may say squawk. In an emergency PHAK says to transmit on 121.5 MHz and set the transponder to 7700. ADS-B uses 978 or 1090 MHz and updates position once a second.
svg.text: Radar, transponder and ADS-B: what ATC sees
The transponder is the airborne portion of the secondary surveillance radar system.
Primary radar and its limits
Measures the time a radio pulse takes to go out
to an object and return; the rotating antenna
position gives the direction
Radio waves normally travel in a straight line
unless bent by atmospheric phenomena such as
temperature inversions
Heavy clouds and precipitation can reflect or
attenuate them, and high terrain can screen them
Signals degrade over distance, cannot penetrate
solid objects such as mountains, and the fastest
radar updates every 4.7 seconds
ATC radar beacon system (ATCRBS)
Often called secondary surveillance radar
Three components: interrogator, transponder,
radarscope
Advantages: reinforcement of radar targets, rapid
target identification, and a unique display of
selected codes
It cannot display the secondary information
unless the aircraft has a transponder
A transponder is required to operate in certain
controlled airspace (PHAK Chapter 15)
Transponder code
4 numbers
each from 0 to 7
possible codes
There are some standard codes, or ATC may issue a
four-digit code. When a controller asks for a code
or function on the transponder, the word "squawk"
may be used.
7700: in an emergency, also transmit the situation on 121.5 MHz (the emergency frequency)
Modes PHAK names
Mode C: altitude reporting transponder mode
Mode A, C and S transponder operations are
associated with the 1090 MHz frequency
ADS-B
ADS-B aircraft exchange information on 978 or
1090 MHz; 978 MHz equipment is the Universal
Access Transceiver (UAT)
1090 MHz transponders with ADS-B add an "extended
squitter" message (1090ES)
Satellite signals do not degrade over distance;
an equipped aircraft updates its own position
once a second
